name: Random-access map benchmark: hash maps vs ordered maps (book companion code)
listed_description: Google Benchmark of random-key lookup on int64 maps of 256 and 1024 elements comparing std::map, std::unordered_map, Abseil btree/flat/node maps, Boost.Container flat_map and Boost.Unordered maps; code in the Chapter-05 folder of the companion repository.
claim_text: Hash maps are universally faster than ordered maps, roughly 10 times faster; lookup time nearly flat with size.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark, uniform random int64 key lookup via operator[], sizes 256 and 1024, AMD Ryzen 7900x; compiler and flags not stated. CPU ns per lookup at 256/1024: std::map 23.3/34.9, std::unordered_map 3.56/3.81, absl::btree_map 19.5/24.1, absl::flat_hash_map 3.81/3.89, absl::node_hash_map 3.95/4.29, boost::container::flat_map 25.9/31.4, boost::unordered_map 3.68/3.66, boost::unordered_flat_map 3.93/4.03. Flat and node hash variants showed no difference, likely because data fit in cache.
found_in: book: The C++ Programmer's Mindset (2025), ch. 5, section Map benchmarks (Table 5.1)

name: Hash function comparison: std::hash vs absl::Hash vs boost::hash (book companion code)
listed_description: Book reports a benchmark in the Chapter-05 code folder comparing std::hash, Abseil hash and Boost hash on integers, doubles and strings under GCC; numbers not printed in the text.
claim_text: On GCC, integer hashing is broadly comparable across the three, but for doubles and strings std::hash is notably slower.
book_benchmark: Benchmark code in the chapter code folder; text gives no numbers, CPU or flags; compiler GCC only.
found_in: book: The C++ Programmer's Mindset (2025), ch. 5, section Hash sets and hash maps

name: csv2
